questions.explain: Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, with sulphur bonded directly to the ring. Benzylsulphonyl chloride (C₆H₅CH₂SO₂Cl) is the common naming trap, and CHCl₃/KOH is the carbylamine reagent.

questions.q: An amine is shaken with C₆H₅SO₂Cl in excess aqueous NaOH. A solid separates that does not dissolve in the alkali and stays insoluble after adding dilute HCl. The amine is:
questions.explain: A secondary amine gives C₆H₅SO₂NR₂, which has no N–H, so it cannot form a salt with NaOH. A primary amine gives an alkali-soluble sulphonamide, and a tertiary amine forms no sulphonamide and dissolves in acid.

questions.q: The sulphonamide C₆H₅SO₂NHC₂H₅ dissolves in aqueous NaOH because:
options: It is hydrolysed back to ethylamine
Its N–H hydrogen is made acidic by the strongly electron-withdrawing SO₂ group
questions.explain: The SO₂ group pulls electron density from nitrogen and stabilises the negative charge left after deprotonation, so NaOH forms the soluble salt C₆H₅SO₂NC₂H₅⁻ Na⁺. Acidifying gives back the insoluble sulphonamide.

questions.q: Triethylamine is subjected to the Hinsberg test under the usual conditions (short shaking at room temperature). What is observed?
options: No sulphonamide forms; the amine stays insoluble in the alkali and dissolves on adding dilute HCl
A clear alkaline solution that precipitates on acidifying
A solid insoluble in both alkali and acid
questions.explain: A tertiary amine has no hydrogen on nitrogen, so it cannot form a stable sulphonamide; it simply dissolves as its salt when acid is added. The clear-then-precipitate pattern belongs to 1° amines and the insoluble solid to 2° amines.
